item.title: Van Hollen, once an insider, has started Democrats' first big fight
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two decades ago, Chris Van Hollen was negotiating in back rooms for Democratic spending priorities and rising through the ranks of the House as a loyal lieutenant to Nancy Pelosi, who saw him as a potential successor. This week, the two-term senator was waging a public challenge to a bid by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) to become Senate majority leader, harnessing grassroots anger and making himself the focal point of Democrats’ first big internal brawl, only weeks after historic midterm election gains. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The turn from insider to outsider did not happen overnight or in a linear fashion. Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, has long shown an ambitious streak, and he has been building a reputation, especially in recent years, as a progressive and increasingly antiestablishment figure. But his underdog challenge to Schumer, 75, has raised his stature on the left and drawn suspicions from detractors that he is using the fight to generate enthusiasm for a potential presidential run, which he denies. “That’s nonsense,” Van Hollen said. “I am not pursuing a bid in 2028.” He noted that the website he created for his leadership bid solicits donations for Democrats who will run to flip Senate seats in 2028. Van Hollen, 67, said his motives are more transparent and sweeping. He wants a Democratic Party that acts more boldly. “One of the things that was very clear in this election is that all of our candidates were running on economic populism,” Van Hollen said in an interview in which he labeled Schumer as the “establishment candidate” in the race. “It wasn’t left or right. It was an understanding that we have an economy that is rigged in favor of very wealthy people and special interests against working people, fueled by political corruption.” The question for Democrats’ next leader, he says, is: “What are you prepared to do?” For Van Hollen, the answer is taking on the “army of lobbyists in Washington” who he fears will “eat away” at the promises Democratic candidates made to take on health insurance companies and other corporate interests. He wants to hold a debate among Democratic senators on changing the filibuster rule so they could pass more legislation with a simple majority, which could allow Democrats to pass a campaign finance overhaul and raise the minimum wage without needing Republican votes. Little of it, in all likelihood, would get Trump’s signature. But it would force a policy confrontation many progressives are craving. Van Hollen’s longshot bid has highlighted Schumer’s weaknesses as many Democrats wonder whether he will face a challenge for his seat from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) in 2028 - or retire. But even a weakened Schumer likely has the upper hand against Van Hollen’s insurgent message. The expanded Democratic caucus includes new lawmakers from red states who distanced themselves from Schumer on the trail, but who may also be wary of backing someone who is running to Schumer’s left. Van Hollen has said he thinks he has at least 15 of the 28 Democratic senator votes he’d need to become leader, and has acknowledged Schumer has the advantage in the race. Only five senators have publicly backed Van Hollen so far, but grassroots activists are calling and urging more to join them. “We have a lot of momentum,” Van Hollen said. From insider to renegade Van Hollen, whose upbringing included stints across the globe as the son of a diplomat, was first elected to public office more than three decades ago, emerging from a crowded primary to win a Maryland House of Delegates seat before taking on his mentor to ascend to the state senate. In 2002 he was elected to the House by toppling the establishment pick from the Kennedy political dynasty, Mark K. Shriver, in the primary. Van Hollen amassed power quickly there, serving as a lead budget negotiator during the Obama administration and twice chairing the House Democrats’ campaign arm. “There were many people in the Congress who thought he might be the next speaker after me,” Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California), said in an interview last year. His Maryland colleague, Donna F. Edwards, then a congresswoman, was part of Van Hollen’s operation to secure support to become the next speaker. But he jettisoned that path in order to run against her for an open Senate seat in 2016. He beat Edwards, who was seen as to the left of Van Hollen on Israel at the time, in a primary she described in an interview as “noxious and toxic.” “This guy, he’s had a challenging election every time he’s moved up,” said former Maryland Attorney General Brian E. Frosh, whose career overlapped with Van Hollen’s. “It’s easy to underestimate him. He’s a giant killer.” In the Senate, Van Hollen was mostly a loyal Democratic foot soldier, helping chair the party’s campaign arm in 2018 and steering millions home to Maryland as a member of the appropriations committee. But in late 2023, Van Hollen began breaking with his party on Israel, increasingly questioning President Joe Biden’s unconditional support as the war with Hamas devolved into a humanitarian crisis in Gaza. In early 2025, when Democrats were reeling from Trump’s win, Van Hollen began criticizing Schumer, and taking bold stands on immigration and Israel that clashed with party orthodoxy. In April that year, he traveled to a notorious El Salvador prison to visit Kilmar Abrego García, a Maryland resident the Trump administration deported to El Salvador despite an order barring his removal there. (Van Hollen was turned away from the prison, but allowed to meet with him at a nearby hotel.) At the time, some Democrats were warning the party should downplay immigration issues and focus on the economy. “That was about taking a courageous stance in the face of the conventional wisdom that now seems very outmoded,” said Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minnesota), who is retiring. In September that year, Van Hollen obliquely criticized Schumer and Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries for failing to endorse Zohran Mamdani in New York, after he had won his primary. “That kind of spineless politics is what people are sick of,” Van Hollen told a crowd of cheering activists in Des Moines. His stances earned him new progressive fans and changed his reputation from insider to rabble rouser. “For a long time he was seen as a kind of consummate inside legislator,” said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee. “And now he is seen as somebody fully in the progressive resistance to Trump and a leader on a whole bunch of different things, including immigration and human rights.” But the substance of that pivot has alienated some longtime supporters. Former state senator Bobby Zirkin, a moderate Democrat, has criticized Van Hollen sharply over Israel since the senator began calling for conditioning military aid to the nation. After Van Hollen announced his leadership plans, Zirkin wrote an op-ed in the Baltimore Sun saying the senator pursued “power over morality.” “He goes where he thinks the wind is going,” Zirkin said in an interview. But Edwards, who battled Van Hollen for his Senate seat and mended fences with him, said in an interview that she encouraged him to challenge Schumer over the summer. “Chris represents the boldness that voters spoke to for this election,” Edwards said. An outside campaign ruffles insider feathers Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan) has also been urging on Van Hollen’s challenge this year, and on Tuesday made the case again to about 100 online influencers. “The most important conversation isn’t just a conversation between 56 senators; it’s a conversation between the 56 senators and the hundreds of millions of people who elected us all,” El-Sayed said in an interview. Van Hollen and his supporters have sought to channel the activist anger with party leadership through groups such as MoveOn and Indivisible, whose leaders have endorsed Van Hollen and whose members are calling their senators to demand they back him, too. “If you were to have a vote today with the Democratic base and say, choose between Senator Schumer and Senator Van Hollen, I would say that Van Hollen would probably win in a landslide,” said Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), who is backing Van Hollen. The tactic has annoyed some lawmakers. It may also have its limits, given the insular nature of the election. Van Hollen’s Democratic colleague from Maryland, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, announced this week that she is supporting Schumer, saying he had asked for her support before Van Hollen entered the race. As online anger with Alsobrooks boiled, Van Hollen released a statement Thursday saying he did not want the discussion around her vote to involve “vitriol or hostility.” Van Hollen has vowed to mostly stay out of Democratic primaries if elected leader, noting that El-Sayed and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota would not be elected if Schumer’s preferred primary candidates had won. Both progressive freshmen are backing Van Hollen. Other newly elected Democrats from more conservative areas worry the dispute could tarnish their efforts to push back on the war, inflation, and other issues that fueled their victories. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-South Carolina) compared the leadership clash to two surgeons arguing about a procedure while a patient was bleeding in the trauma bay. “Really what we need is someone just to stop the bleeding,” she told reporters. Andrews has not said whom she is supporting. Theodoric Meyer contributed to this report. item.title: RFK Jr. vows to curb a measles crisis he initially underestimated
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Hours after the United States lost its measles-elimination status, erasing a landmark public health victory earned 26 years ago, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. declared the country would fight the spread of the disease. "We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status," Kennedy posted on X. "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But as federal and state governments confront the spread of one of the world's most contagious diseases, some state and local officials question whether Kennedy and his department can bring it under control. Kennedy had sowed doubt about the safety of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine for years and, as the top U.S. health official, has sought major changes to childhood immunization policy, to cheers from some supporters of his Make America Healthy Again movement. Those actions, some public health experts say, have complicated efforts to persuade more Americans to get vaccinated and rebuild the population immunity needed to bring outbreaks under control. As federal health agencies deployed resources to West Texas in 2025, Kennedy initially underestimated the resurgence of the disease, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal matters. "It took him a while to accept measles as something that wasn't going to go away quickly," said a former health official. Federal health officials must now develop a corrective action plan for the Pan American Health Organization, the regional health agency that withdrew the U.S.'s measles elimination status, outlining how the country will stop continuous spread of the virus and regain its status. PAHO officials said they expect the plan in the coming weeks, although there is no formal deadline. Even before the U.S. officially lost its designation, federal officials began taking steps toward that effort. Erica Schwartz, the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, met earlier this month with public health groups to discuss strategies for curbing the outbreaks and to identify challenges, according to two public health officials with knowledge of the meeting who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. The CDC, state health officials, epidemiologists and national immunization groups are also planning regional meetings to coordinate the response, with special attention to improving outreach to vulnerable communities. The Department of Health and Human Services said it has been aggressive in fighting measles. Since August, the CDC has made $100 million available to states to improve the response. It has provided help from CDC scientists to states battling outbreaks, including Texas, South Carolina, New York, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. "We will address PAHO's findings directly," HHS spokeswoman Emily Hilliard said in a statement. "HHS and CDC will address the findings and work with partners to document interruption of endemic transmission and meet the requirements for re-achieving elimination status." State and local health officials say they welcome those efforts. But stopping continuous spread of the virus requires a broader and sustained effort, including raising vaccination rates in communities where coverage has fallen before Kennedy came into office. Only the federal government can do what states cannot do on their own, such as coordinate across states, bring health and immunization officials together, and provide robust funding and expertise. New York's health commissioner, James McDonald, said at a briefing Thursday with reporters that PAHO's decision was expected well in advance, and a federal plan should have already been prepared. "I'm already concerned that Health and Human Services does not have a national plan," McDonald said. New York, which declared a state disaster emergency in response to its outbreak, recorded a measles-related child death - its first in over 30 years - earlier this month. Others say losing elimination status should itself prompt a strong response across all levels of government. "I do hope it's a wake-up call for CDC, for Congress, for HHS, for everyone," said Claire Hannan, the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers. "We need to be doing more." A growing outbreak As the founder of a prominent anti-vaccine group, Kennedy had for years raised questions about the safety of the MMR vaccine. He previously linked the shot to autism despite decades of contradictory evidence. And he wrote in a book that measles outbreaks have been "fabricated" to "inflict unnecessary and risky vaccines" on millions of children. As the West Texas outbreak grew in early 2025, Kennedy coupled messages encouraging vaccination with false or misleading claims about the MMR vaccine. He promoted alternative treatments and questioned whether a child who state health officials said died of measles had actually died of the disease. His claims that vaccines contain "aborted fetus debris and DNA particles" prompted Debra Houry, the CDC's then-chief medical officer, to send information to "help him with his talking points," according to an email she sent to senior CDC officials on May 1, 2025. "Even though fetal cells are used to grow vaccine viruses, vaccines do not contain these cells or pieces of DNA that are recognizable as human DNA," she wrote to then-CDC chief of staff Matt Buzzelli and others. "Vaccines also do not contain fetal cells," she added. Kennedy's statements stood in contrast to how prior health officials messaged around vaccinations by imploring Americans to get vaccinated, including during President Donald Trump's first term. Then-Health Secretary Alex Azar said communities had been the subject of "mass disinformation campaigns. … They need to get their kids vaccinated." Public health experts say controlling outbreaks requires clear, repeated messages about vaccination, while acknowledging that declining trust in the CDC since the coronavirus pandemic has made federal officials less effective messengers. The CDC has not held a news briefing for reporters since Jan. 20, when the then-principal deputy director, Ralph Abraham, was asked whether losing elimination status would be significant and replied: "Not really. … You know, it's just the cost of doing business." The health department has maintained that Kennedy has "repeatedly stated that MMR vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles infection" and that "any notion that the Trump Administration is discouraging measles vaccination is absolutely fake news." Two doses of the shot provide 97 percent protection against measles. Over the last year, dozens of measles outbreaks have taken hold across the country, and nationwide case counts have continued to climb. In West Texas, there were 762 cases during the 2025 outbreak. In South Carolina, the outbreak totaled 997 before it was declared over in April. And in Pennsylvania, officials have recorded 1,631 cases, including eight deaths, as of Friday. In July, the U.S. reported the most measles cases in 35 years, surpassing last year's record total. The resurgence, now totaling more than 5,800 cases nationwide, is posing myriad challenges for doctors and state health officials. Vaccine uptake has been declining for years amid rising skepticism. Meanwhile, outbreaks in traditionally undervaccinated communities are becoming harder to quickly extinguish. Many doctors have never seen cases of measles, prompting health departments to educate clinicians on the basics and hospitals to quickly craft new protocols to safely isolate patients with a virus that can remain suspended in the air for up to two hours. "Some of these outbreaks we've been seeing recently, for example, in Pennsylvania, it's not just kids who are getting sick," said Adriane Casalotti, who heads government and public affairs for the National Association of County and City Health Officials. "In fact, there's many more adults who are contracting measles, and that shows a longer pattern of undervaccination." When immunizations in the broader population are high, it's easier to protect communities with lower vaccination rates. But that's not necessarily the case anymore, Casalotti said. Pennsylvania has the largest measles outbreak in the country. But it's also been the center of a bitter political feud between Kennedy and Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat widely viewed as a presidential contender. When Pennsylvania reported its first two measles-associated deaths in 35 years in August, Kennedy suggested the deaths "may even have been altogether fabricated," and he accused Shapiro of using the moment for political gain. It wasn't the first time Kennedy had disputed the official state account of deaths; he questioned whether measles caused the death of one of the two Texas children who died during the 2025 outbreak. Houry said such statements by Kennedy can leave the public with the impression that "maybe the disease isn't that deadly or that serious." The CDC's Schwartz made the unusual decision to exclude those first deaths from the national tally, departing from the agency's practice of relying on state health departments to make those determinations. The agency has since added some deaths from Pennsylvania and says it is working with outside partners to craft a new definition of deaths due to measles. The gap between federal and state counts has persisted as the toll has grown: States have now reported at least 11 measles-associated deaths this year in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York. The CDC's tally is six. Can the U.S. regain its status? Kennedy's allies argue he should not be blamed for the rising cases of measles in the U.S., pointing to a worldwide resurgence and vaccine uptake that declined amid the covid pandemic. Other countries have lost their elimination status and regained it after years of work. Venezuela lost its status in 2018 and regained it in 2023. Brazil regained its designation in November 2024, about five years after losing it. Canada, which lost its status last year, has since stopped the continuous spread that cost it the designation, PAHO officials said. But it must go at least 12 months without measles spreading continuously before it can regain its status. State and local health officials say regaining elimination status will require a national strategy that accounts for widely varying conditions on the ground. States with large ongoing outbreaks, such as Pennsylvania, require a different response from places that have kept high vaccination rates and are trying to prevent the virus from gaining a foothold. In some communities where outbreaks are occurring, such as areas with Amish and Mennonite populations, some parents aren't necessarily opposed to vaccination or hesitant, but they don't get their children vaccinated because they don't routinely seek medical care. Yet some public health experts fear the rhetoric in the second Trump administration could dissuade parents from getting their children vaccinated. Kennedy's approach to vaccines is part of a broader push within the Trump administration to reduce and space out the shots children receive. While the administration has continued to recommend the MMR vaccine, Trump has suggested the combination vaccine could be "lethal," while acknowledging that he had no scientific evidence for the claim. He has said the vaccine should be broken up into three disease-specific shots, which medical groups say would offer no health benefit and could leave children vulnerable to more diseases for longer. The changes have been embraced by some activists in the MAHA movement that helped propel Kennedy into office even as major medical organizations have condemned them. That creates a difficult dynamic as Kennedy tries to regain a public health designation that depends heavily on increasing vaccination, public health experts say. The U.S. eliminated continuous measles transmission in 2000 through a combination of federal and state efforts, said Daniel Edney, president of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials. States imposed vaccination requirements for schools, and the federal government created the Vaccines for Children program, which provides vaccines to about half the children in the U.S. "Everybody was pulling together the same way," Edney said. "There was no dissension. The medical community was in alignment with public health, who was in alignment with the CDC … and everybody was working toward the same goal." Caitlin Gilbert contributed to this report. - - - Graphics: Reported measles cases in the U.S., 2000 to 2026 Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/21/rfk-jr-vows-curb-measles-crisis-he-initially-underestimated/

item.title: Jan. 6 leader who once backed Trump now says he's 'absolutely done'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
IRVING, Texas (AP) — Stewart Rhodes didn’t just go to prison for Donald Trump . While serving time for his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, the founder of the right-wing militia known as the Oath Keepers got a tattoo of Trump’s defiant face after he survived an assassin’s bullet in Butler, Pennsylvania . It was further proof of Rhodes' devotion to the Republican president. But that's all over now. “I am absolutely done with Trump,” said Rhodes, sitting at a rickety yellow table outside a gastropub in Irving, Texas. He considers Trump not just a traitor, but "one of the very worst in our nation's history.” The repudiation from a former acolyte — one convicted of seditious conspiracy for orchestrating an ill-fated attempt to keep Trump in power six years ago — is another example of how allegiance to the president has faded even among extreme supporters. Back then, Rhodes claimed Trump lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden because of election fraud. This year in Texas, where Democrats had historic victories , he said there's another reason. “The lion’s share is because Trump pissed off his own base," Rhodes said, his face shaded by a black cowboy hat. An eye patch covers his left socket, the result of an old gun accident, and a glacial blue iris peers out from the other. Nearby, people mingled with drinks for his Christian Warriors After-Party, organized during a three-day conference called “Christ is King: America After Trump.” Some people approached to shake hands or sign up for the Oath Keepers or trainings for things like community defense and hurricane relief. ‘The first inkling’ of a split from Trump The beginning of Rhodes' break with Trump came when the president gave pardons to hundreds of people who were locked up for their actions on Jan. 6, 2021, but only commuted Rhodes' sentence . “That was the first inkling,” Rhodes said. Rhodes also said Trump's war with Iran violated Trump's promises to end foreign conflicts. And, Rhodes said, it felt like an affront when Trump dismissed people who urged his administration to release files about the Jeffrey Epstein case , calling them “PAST supporters.” Then Rhodes felt Trump went back on his longtime slogan. “We elected him to end the corruption in Washington, D.C. ‘Drain the swamp.’ Unfortunately his administration has been one of the most corrupt administrations in U.S. history," Rhodes said. “The pardons are pay-for-play and everything is pay-for-play.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Rhodes is not alone in his about-face on Trump, but there's an ideological through line, said Sam Jackson, an associate professor at the University at Albany with a focus on anti-government extremism. “They went from seeing Donald Trump as their ally in this fight against the conspiracy, to actually being co-opted by the conspiracy,” Jackson said, and it “points to deeper consistency in that understanding of the world as driven by hidden, evil actors.” Rhodes, who graduated from Yale Law School and worked for former U.S. Rep. Ron Paul of Texas, founded the Oath Keepers in 2009 with the goal of encouraging members of the military and law enforcement to resist what they view as unconstitutional orders, such as disarming citizens or carrying out warrantless searches. Watching from prison when Trump was fired on Rhodes later allied himself with Trump's political movement, and the Oath Keepers supported his attempt to remain in office after losing the 2020 election. Fueled with conspiracies about voter fraud, prosecutors said group members gathered weapons, organized trainings and assembled in Washington , where some helped storm the Capitol on Jan. 6. Rhodes, who did not enter the building that day, said he was a “political prisoner" who faced “illegality” in his trial. He was sentenced to 18 years, one of the longest sentences of any Jan. 6 case. “You are smart, you are charismatic and compelling and frankly that’s what makes you dangerous,” U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta said during the hearing. “The moment you are released, whenever that may be, you will be ready to take up arms against your government.” Rhodes was behind bars as Trump began his political comeback. He said he watched the assassination attempt in Butler on a prison television with other inmates. He saw Trump pump his fist and yell “fight,” and he figured that God’s hand was on the man. After Trump won the 2024 election, he swiftly pardoned hundreds of people convicted of crimes related to Jan. 6, including those who assaulted police officers. Rhodes received a commutation, which didn’t wipe his record clean. “He let us out of prison. We were grateful. I didn’t get a pardon though,” he said. Tattoo that honored Trump will be ‘modified’ to reflect a new reality The Justice Department vacated Rhodes' conviction earlier this year, lifting his felon status. Rhodes said he's working to rebuild the Oath Keepers, which previously had tens of thousands of members, according to leaked lists. With his rights restored, Rhodes said his first priority was to get some guns, and he didn't register to vote in time for the election. But he said he wouldn't have cast a ballot anyway. That's because Rhodes felt that “the Republican Party has taken us for granted," and he didn't want to choose between “a half a dose of poison or a full dose.” As for his tattoo of Trump, the man he now considers a traitor, Rhodes has plans that he didn't specify. “I will have this prison tattoo of Trump ‘modified,'” he wrote in a text message, “to reflect that reality. That treason.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/oath-keepers-founder-jan-6-130043975.html

item.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks have increased to highest level since Iran war began
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Reported attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been higher in number in October and November than any previous months since the war between the U.S., Israel and Iran began in late February , according to data compiled by maritime organizations. The attacks appear to be a bid to complicate U.S.-led efforts to keep oil flowing through the economically crucial Strait of Hormuz despite an Iranian-declared blockade, experts told ABC News. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 31 attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October, and about 19 in November, as of Nov. 18. Noppadon Wongsuvan via AP Photo - PHOTO: Smoke billows from the Mayuree Naree, a Thailand-flagged bulk carrier, after it was hit by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, north of Oman, on March 11, 2026. Previously, a total of 53 incidents had been reported to the UKMTO between March and September of this year, averaging 10 to 15 incidents total across both Strait of Hormuz and surrounding gulfs in previous months. The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a United Nations agency, has slightly more conservative numbers, with 34 attacks confirmed in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October and November so far. This too, is still a marked increase from previous numbers the IMO had collected, which number roughly 50 in and around the Strait of Hormuz between March and September. The IMO has tallied 138 attacks on vessels in total across the Middle East since the war began. The positions of attacked tankers reported to the UKMTO indicate that most attacked vessels were in the very southern portion of the Strait of Hormuz, staying close to the Omani coastline, according to the maritime group's data. Social media via Reuters - PHOTO: Smoke rises at sea off the coast of Oman, Nov. 18, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. What experts say Iran aims to accomplish "Iran's objective remains to keep the Omani route, which is described as a U.S.-facilitated route, a very high-risk passage and to keep the energy recovery inconsistent," Noam Raydan, senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told ABC News. Felt Maps/UKMTO/Verified UGC - PHOTO: Map identifying locations where vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October and November of 2026, according to UKMTO data. "Washington and its regional partners have found ways to keep oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told ABC News. "Tehran now seems determined to make these arrangements more costly and less reliable." The workaround developed by the U.S. involves "ship-to-ship" (STS) transfers in which smaller tankers cross the strait with tracking systems switched off, and transfer cargos to larger tankers once safely on the other side, Sina Toossi, senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, told ABC News. Iran is now responding in "a cycle of adaptation and counter-adaptation," he said. "Tehran has escalated its attacks to make the STS system more dangerous, costly, and ultimately unviable. Iran's broader objective is to demonstrate that normal oil exports cannot continue while the US maintains its blockade of Iran, and to generate enough economic pressure to force Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict," Toossi said. The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade, stopping Iranian and Iran-linked ships from going in and out of the Gulf of Oman, starting April 13, with a brief pause from June 18 to July 13. Anadolu via Getty Images - PHOTO: Commercial vessels and oil tankers sit anchored in the waters off Bandar Abbas in southern Iran's Hormozgan Province on Sept. 9, 2026. Attacks not isolated to ships crossing the strait Strikes have not been limited to ships. On Nov. 8, Iran attacked the Omani island of Didamar in the strait itself, according to satellite images and video verified by ABC News. The island hosts radar and satellite communications technology. Iranian state media said Iran had struck what it described as "enemy navigation aid systems." Oman, a U.S. partner, did not comment on the attack. Copernicus Sentinel 2 - PHOTO: Satellite image of Oman's Didamar island in the Strait of Hormuz following claimed Iranian attacks on infrastructure on the island. Strikes have also not been isolated to ships actively crossing the strait. ABC News has verified at least one incident in which a ship was attacked by a drone appearing to belong to Iran, despite not making any attempt to cross the strait. In early October, the Panama-flagged supertanker Gem No. 2 had been idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in the Persian Gulf, outside the Strait of Hormuz, for nearly five months. It was fully loaded with a cargo of two million barrels of Saudi crude oil, per maritime intelligence company Kpler, and was one of the hundreds of ships the International Maritime Organization estimates is stuck in the Persian Gulf since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. What happened to Gem No. 2? Two crew members who were on board Gem No. 2 say the ship never attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz, and that it was attacked by one drone on Oct. 9 and then at least three others on Oct. 10, the latter attack sparking a massive fire and forcing the ship's evacuation, according to videos filmed by the crew obtained and verified by ABC News. Obtained by ABC News - PHOTO: Oil Tanker Gem No2 on fire after being hit by drones while sitting idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in October 2026. Hours after the vessel was struck for a second time and evacuated, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in an online post that the vessel had struck a naval mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route. Satellite images taken in the days after it was abandoned confirm Gem No. 2's position off the coast of the UAE, well outside the Strait of Hormuz. Copernicus Sentinel 2 - PHOTO: Satellite image of oil tanker Gem No2 off the coast of the UAE on October 24, two weeks after being attacked. ABC News showed images taken by the crew of the wreckage of the drone that struck the ship on Oct. 9 to Fabian Hinz, a researcher who studies drone warfare. Hinz said the wreckage in the images belongs to a jet-powered Hadid-110, built by Iran. Iran continues to say the ship hit a mine. Large tankers targeted: Analyst Azizi, the ICG's Iran analyst, suggested that "large oil tankers seem to be receiving particular attention, whether they are moving through the strait or operating elsewhere in the Persian Gulf." "One possible explanation is that Tehran wants to discourage the use of supertankers and prevent the development of alternative shipping arrangements that could make the blockade less effective," he said. Obtained by ABC News - PHOTO: Pieces of a drone that hit oil tanker Gem No2 on October 9th, identified as an Iranian Hadid-110 drone by an expert to ABC News. It's not clear why Gem No. 2 was allegedly targeted, but the vessel would have been an easy target, according to Samir Madani, co-founder of TankerTrackers.c o m . Madani told ABC News he noticed Gem No. 2 before the attack because the tanker's location transmission services were turned on, revealing its location publicly. Both Azizi and Toossi describe Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz as having "strategic logic." "Ultimately, the objective goes beyond disrupting oil exports. item.title: Anthropic engineer proposes a theory for all these outages
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
There have been so many prominent tech services experiencing outages lately that the problems have gone mainstream in a new way we haven't seen before. Besides the headlines and podcasts (some of which are asking if this is actually a new thing or if we're just noticing it more), the tech outages have kept Vice President JD Vance from attending New York events , led to the resignation of the White House's cybersecurity chief , made “Saturday Night Live,” and been the subject of tons of memes and TikTok comedy where people joke that "LinkedIn and Tinder must be down, because I'm not getting any responses!" As we wrote recently , the problems are far more than just cybersecurity, though AI means hackers can discover and exploit bugs like never before. Infrastructure is decrepit. Maintenance is deferred. Exhausted, too-small teams of IT workers aren't up to this level of chaos. But there's another explanation that's perhaps underappreciated: one big downside of Claude Code, the marquee product that has given Anthropic ( ANT ) its trillion-dollar valuation. The problem is best explained by someone who would know best: a prominent Anthropic engineer (and former Google engineer) who works on Claude Code as a member of the technical staff, Addy Osmani, whose treatise on " comprehension debt " bounced around the software engineering community in March — and is even more relevant today. What Osmani highlights isn't really a weakness in Claude Code, but in how companies and engineering teams use it. The gist: AI can write code faster than we can review it. The speed is a great benefit, but it's also a curse, as myriad companies pivot from writing code to overseeing teams of AI agents that complain less and write more. As Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week , the company's engineers "build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product." Dario Amodei is seen on the display at the Nasdaq MarketSite as shares of Anthropic begin trading after their IPO in Times Square, New York City, United States, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Stephanie Keith/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto via Getty Images Traditionally, the laborious process of checking other people's code is how software engineers internalize why systems are designed the way they are, and why decisions from earlier in a project might be meaningful today. But reviewing the entirety of AI code isn't feasible given how fast we can produce it now. It's too unwieldy, and this represents a massive bottleneck for progress. Tests, AI review, and spending less time reviewing can be effective. But they've removed layers of verification, and ultimately comprehension, which is disappearing, Osmani explains. All this means that with code piling up faster than humans can review it, companies can lose control of their systems in a way far more prosaic and banal than some sort of sentient AI or Skynet doomsday scenario. With human code proofreaders at their limits, when things inevitably break , that missing understanding matters. Coders — or even AI — may not realize that a few lines of code represent an important piece of figurative duct tape, a load-bearing wall, or a mechanism that triggers other contingencies. Every patch or attempted fix can also break more things. That brings us back to the wave of cyber outages . Aside from a few high-profile lawsuits and public scandals, the tech giants whose software "ate the world" and that now commandeer our attention spans have largely escaped meaningful accountability. Their software failures are embarrassing. And their design choices have led to allegations of addiction, anti-social behavior, and economic exploitation. But they have, generally speaking, escaped rigorous regulation. AI changes the calculus. The era of honor system self-policing may be coming to an end. "When AI-generated code is running in healthcare systems, financial infrastructure, and government services," Osmani wrote, the excuse that an AI wrote bad code and we didn't fully review it "will not hold up in a post-incident report when lives or significant assets are at stake." Cyber outages are often a nuisance and, mercifully, haven't led to a mass-casualty event or prolonged economic crisis. But in a world where AI can generate code faster than anyone can keep up, it's not hard to imagine that changing. item.title: At least 11 people killed in Mexico's Sinaloa after capture of cartel boss, officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — A burst of violence in Mexico’s Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday. Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after an intense firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning. Mexico’s Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed. The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms. Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores. He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos,” a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state. Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups. As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions. Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city. Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. “The fighting was happening all over Guasave,” said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. “It spread throughout the city.” Mexican authorities said that they used “stealth and surprise” to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities. Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to discuss the case. “Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary,” the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least “10 roadblocks” with burning vehicles on Guasave’s streets. Terror in Sinaloa Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations. “Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks,” Sánchez told The Associated Press. She said that the city’s firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning. An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation. Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday. “The aftermath of last night’s war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down,” Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico. Guasave residents remained “very afraid” because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said. Capture prompts celebration and warnings Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office. The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities. “Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. “We will continue the hunt.” Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention “an important step in pacifying Sinaloa.” Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins , including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes , known as “ El Mencho ,” who was killed by the military in February. Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run. The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa. “What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States,” Saucedo said. “What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.” ___ Janetsky and Sánchez reported from Mexico City. Associated Press writer Thomas Strong contributed to this report from Washington. item.title: COP31 climate summit risks failure as talks go deep into overtime
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The COP31 climate summit will either produce a good deal or no deal at all, the European Union's top climate official said on Saturday as talks stretched deep into overtime. Negotiators from ‌nearly 200 countries are struggling to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, delaying an agreement at the two-week conference ‌that had been scheduled to end on Friday. "It's either going to be a good deal or it's going to be no deal," EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told reporters. Asked about ​the chances of no deal emerging, he said: "We will find out." The last major breakdown in UN climate talks came in Copenhagen in 2009, when countries failed to adopt the Copenhagen Accord by consensus in a setback for multilateral climate diplomacy. As workers dismantled catering stands and exhibits at the venue, delegations shuttled between meeting rooms to discuss tactics, while others rested as they awaited a new version of the negotiating text. Turkey's COP31 President Murat Kurum met officials ‌from the EU, Australia and Saudi Arabia in an ⁠effort to break the deadlock, but acknowledged a deal could prove elusive. "I call on every country to act responsibly," he told reporters. "There is no benefit for anyone to ruin this process by getting hung up on words, phrases." The ⁠biggest sticking points are whether a final agreement should mention the fossil fuels driving global warming and whether it should include support for poorer countries adapting to climate change. A draft deal published on Thursday removed earlier references to ending fossil fuel use. Observers said Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers ​had ​opposed the language. The draft also dropped a proposed $120 billion target for finance to help ​developing countries adapt to climate change. Negotiators had expected a ‌revised draft on Friday. But by Saturday afternoon, with no new text on the table, hopes for significant changes had faded and frustration was mounting. DELAYS Recent climate summits have regularly overrun without collapsing, eventually producing agreements. Isatou Camara, Gambia's finance negotiator, said some countries appeared to be using delay tactics to pressure others into accepting a weaker outcome. "This delay strategy which has been used at previous COPs could be so at the end when things are put on the table you accept because you are fed up, exhausted, and want to go home," she said. This year's talks have been further ‌complicated by war and rising living costs, which are competing for the attention of ​policymakers and the public. The US, the world's largest historical greenhouse gas emitter, is also ​absent from the talks for the second year in a row ​after President Donald Trump ended cooperation on climate policy, calling global warming a hoax. A UN report last month found ‌the world is on track to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 ​degrees Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial ​levels, a threshold governments agreed under the 2015 Paris Agreement to try to avoid breaching. The draft agreement acknowledges that projected overshoot and calls for faster deployment of technologies that remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere to help bring temperatures back down. Some delegations opposed including ​carbon-removal technologies, arguing that doing so could open the ‌door to continued fossil fuel use. "The fact there is loads of unfinished business at this COP shows there's a big problem ​here," said Brenda Mwale, Malawi's loss and damage negotiator. "The question is are we in a leadership crisis? Was there really ​a vision for this COP?" (Writing by Richard Valdmanis. item.title: Bayer agrees to pay up to $7.25 billion over Roundup cancer claims spanning decades
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge. The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness. For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users. Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements. Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling. In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are “fair and adequate” and the total dollar amount is “among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.” The approved settlement includes $600 million for attorneys' fees. The judge said there was a risk Bayer would have filed for bankruptcy protection if the settlement had been rejected. Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation." The decision could be appealed. Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer’s deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less. The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens. Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as “probably carcinogenic” in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it’s not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed. About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets. The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion. In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court’s precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict “should send a strong signal” that plaintiffs “will face significant challenges” pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer’s U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader. Attorneys disagree on whether the settlement is fair Bayer previously set aside $16 billion to cover legal costs related to Roundup cases. The new settlement, which is in addition to that, is designed to address most of the remaining lawsuits, as well as any additional cases brought in the coming years by people who were exposed to Roundup before the settlement was proposed in February. “Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case. The settlement calls for Bayer to make annual payments into a special fund for up to 21 years, totaling as much as $7.25 billion. The amount of money paid out to individuals would vary. Agricultural, industrial or turf workers exposed at length to Roundup could receive an average of $165,000 if they were diagnosed with an aggressive form of the illness while younger than age 60. But anyone diagnosed at age 78 or older would get significantly less, with an average of $10,000. Some attorneys have said the individual settlement amounts are too small and the terms too restrictive. “This settlement is the scariest, worst future settlement that’s ever been contemplated,” attorney Gerson Smoger said during a September court hearing on whether the settlement was fair. He said it locked in future claimants for decades with no chance at punitive damages yet “kept the product that they were exposed to on the market, allowing the victims to continue to be exposed.” The settlement was filed in St. Louis Circuit Court in Missouri, home to Bayer’s North America crop science division and the state where many of the lawsuits have been brought. item.title: Visitors leave tributes after Fiona the hippo dies in freak accident at Cincinnati Zoo
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A necropsy has revealed that the knit cap responsible for the death of the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo Fiona was lodged so deep in her digestive tract that she effectively had no chance of survival. Zoo officials said on Friday that the hat got stuck 25 feet beyond Fiona's final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines. "Upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object," explained Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health. "The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked." Fiona's mother, Bibi, and the zoo's other hippos, Tucker and Fritz, "are eating and behaving normally," said Christina Gorsuch, the zoo's director of animal care. "It's difficult to know how they're feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves." "Keepers, vets, staff, and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss," the zoo said. "She meant a lot to a lot of people." It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency. https://t.co/X0GVbDAiEQ pic.twitter.com/7wLF0uclWB — Cincinnati Zoo (@CincinnatiZoo) November 19, 2026 The zoo announced Fiona's death on Thursday, 11 days after she swallowed a hat that had slipped into her enclosure. She was 9 years old. "It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said in a statement. Fans near and far have been grieving ever since. Thane Maynard, executive chair of the zoo's board, compared Fiona to "lightning in a bottle," adding that he had "never known an animal so beloved in all my life." On Friday, zoo visitors draped a hippo statue with flowers and notes written in crayon, according to the Associated Press . A young girl held up a drawing of Fiona; someone else left behind a watermelon, one of Fiona's favorite treats. Flowers, handwritten notes, watermelons and other items are displayed at a memorial for Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo. AP Photo/Obed Lamy Flowers and cards rest by a statue outside the Cincinnati Zoo. AP Photo/Sallee Ann Harrison Jessica Grieshop, who often visited Fiona with her daughters, called the hippo an inspiration for "anyone that was going through hard times." Cincinnati landmarks, including stadiums and bridges, were lit purple Thursday night in Fiona's honor. The zoo asked people not to send flowers or gifts and instead "honor Fiona by spreading love and cheer to those around you." It is accepting memorial donations . Local businesses are raising money, too. Cincinnati bakery chain Servatii is selling $1 "Fiona Donuts" this weekend, with all proceeds going to the zoo, WKRC reported . The zoo's Hippo Cove is closed through the weekend. The zoo's animal care team spent days trying to help Fiona pass the obstruction, going so far as to use a vibration plate borrowed from a horse farm to help shake it through her digestive tract. An ultrasound showed bunching in Fiona's intestines; a colonoscopy with a 9-foot scope didn't help, nor did a "giant" enema. "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "We are in shock at the moment. We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore." Specialists said surgery wasn't an option for a full-grown Nile hippopotamus. "They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don't regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does," Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, told the Associated Press . "Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid and digesting food easily 'hide' the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult." Hippos are also difficult to anesthetize and keep away from water as they heal. Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told reporters that Fiona ingested the knit hat on Nov. 8 after it was tossed in the air by a child and flung by a ceiling fan through a 1-foot opening above the viewing windows of her enclosure. "We probably couldn't make that happen again if we tried," Curley said at the time. "It was clearly an accident." In the days that followed, Fiona's appetite started to wane. Fiona was no stranger to health struggles; she became a sensation after she was born six weeks premature in 2017. At the time, she couldn't stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds; the next smallest Nile hippo on record weighed roughly twice as much at birth. Fiona in 2020. John Minchillo/AP No one expected Fiona to survive. Zoo staff had to bottle-feed her with a mixture of formula and her mother's milk. (A hippopotamus had never been hand-milked before.) While teething, Fiona began to refuse the bottle, and clinicians from Cincinnati Children's Hospital were called in to administer fluids intravenously. But eventually Fiona began to thrive. Named after Shrek's love interest, Princess Fiona — zoo staff thought her ears had a similar shape — she went on to star in her own show on YouTube and other platforms. Her plight — and her adorable triumph over adversity — inspired a host of children's books, a line of beer, a bobblehead and even a limited-edition ice cream flavor. She weighed nearly 2,500 pounds when she died. Fiona also became a Cincinnati icon. Her character in the Cincinnati Ballet's 2018 production of Nutcracker reportedly " stole the show "; the same year, a Fiona mural was unveiled downtown. Fiona's death sparked a series of tributes. The Cincinnati Bengals wrote in a post on X, "Rest in peace, Fiona. The queen of the Queen City." Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno added his tribute, saying, "Fiona wasn't just Cincinnati's hippo, she was Ohio's fighter. Born tiny, premature, and against every odd, she grew up and brought pure joy to millions of us." second lady Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, shared an undated photo of one of their children gazing at Fiona through the glass of her enclosure. "We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona," Vance wrote. "Our family loved visiting her at the Cincinnati Zoo." "Our city is heartbroken," Mayor Aftab Pureval wrote on social media, "but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole." "Our hearts are with the staff of the Cincinnati Zoo and everyone who loved her," added outgoing Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine. "She will be deeply missed." Amy Acton, Ohio's incoming governor, said that Fiona's survival story "brought joy, hope and a little extra magic to our state." On Friday, Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno introduced a resolution honoring Fiona and the Cincinnati Zoo staff on the floor of the U.S. Senate. It passed unanimously. Fiona was Ohio’s little fighter from day one and I’m proud that my resolution honoring her passed the Senate UNANIMOUSLY. My heart goes out to the amazing team at the @CincinnatiZoo who cared for her. Rest easy, Fiona. Ohio loves you. pic.twitter.com/G0ln1rSRRF — Bernie Moreno (@berniemoreno) November 20, 2026 "Fiona was a symbol of resilience, of perseverance, and we're going to miss her in Cincinnati," Moreno said. Her loss, he added, will "leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in the heart." item.title: More trouble for Nvidia as SEC reportedly probes accounting amid historic stock slide
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books. Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss, before bouncing nearly 4% in after-hours trading. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment. The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $490 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ). Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee. Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China. Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on. Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership . California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said. The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market. Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report. "Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.
